title: Fractional parts of powers of 3/2 are complex and apparently random

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Fractional parts of powers of 3/2 are complex and apparently random

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The fractional parts of successive powers of 3/2, a base-independent measure of size, show the same complexity and apparent randomness that appears in their digit sequences.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: they too exhibit the kind of complexity and apparent randomness that is evident at the level of digits.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Elementary Arithmetic” (from p. 117), p. 121. Scope: fractional parts of (3/2)^n

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Exact or high-precision terms can be generated without new empirical data and standard distribution tests are feasible. Finite computation cannot settle all asymptotic randomness properties, leaving the broad statement only partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute high-precision fractional parts of (3/2)^n and test their distribution, serial correlations, discrepancy, and compressibility against explicit random alternatives. Deviations reject the selected randomness model, while agreement supports only the tested finite-scale interpretation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Apparent randomness lacks a unique criterion.

The asymptotic distribution of fractional parts is not settled by finite samples.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.62
operationalizability: 0.68
data existence: 0.95
data adequacy: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.92

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fractional parts of successive powers of 3/2 are a concrete, base-independent sequence and can be computed for millions of terms with public arbitrary-precision arithmetic. The claim is about apparent complexity and randomness, which standard tests on those terms can support or, if a pattern appears, refute. A proof of equidistribution is not required for the practical reading Wolfram gives.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute the fractional parts of (3/2)^n to high precision for a large range of n and test them for equidistribution, autocorrelation, and lattice structure. Visible large-scale order would refute apparent randomness; agreement with randomness diagnostics on a long prefix would confirm the practical claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Equidistribution of {(3/2)^n} is a stronger open statement than the practical appearance claim.

High powers need carefully controlled precision, and rounding error can imitate or hide structure.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.85
data adequacy: 0.75
data existence: 0.9
operationalizability: 0.75
